messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 65

# The Weight of a Uniform

Marcus is a 46-year-old graphic designer who lives with his wife in a mid-sized European city. He is soft-spoken and precise in the way he describes things — a man accustomed to thinking in images, in composition, in the exact placement of elements. It is perhaps this quality that makes what happened to him so difficult to escape. He cannot stop seeing it.

Three years ago, Marcus was walking home from a late client meeting when he was stopped by two police officers in a poorly lit side street. What began as a routine identity check escalated within seconds. One officer, apparently convinced Marcus matched the description of a suspect, shoved him against a brick wall, forced his arms behind his back, and pressed a forearm hard against the back of his neck. Marcus remembers the cold of the stone against his cheek, the inability to breathe properly, and the sound of his own voice — high and strange — saying he couldn't move, that he wasn't resisting. He was held there for nearly twenty minutes before a third officer arrived and confirmed the mistake. No apology was offered. He was told to go home.

Marcus drove himself to an urgent care clinic that night for bruising along his ribs and a strained shoulder. He told his wife it had been an accident. He didn't fully explain what happened for almost two months.

In the weeks that followed, he found himself unable to sleep past three in the morning. He would lie in the dark with his heart hammering, replaying the sensation of being pinned, of having no control over what was happening to his body. He began avoiding the street where it occurred — then the entire neighbourhood — then, gradually, any area where he might encounter uniformed officers. He stopped taking evening client meetings. He began working exclusively from home, telling himself it was more efficient, though his wife noticed he had stopped going out at all after dark.

At work, Marcus sits at his desk for hours and produces almost nothing. Projects that once excited him — brand identities, editorial layouts, anything requiring sustained visual thinking — now feel unreachable. He opens files and stares at them. He describes it as trying to think through wet concrete. His clients have noticed delays. He has lost two long-standing accounts in the past year and cannot bring himself to pursue new ones.

When Marcus sees a police vehicle in traffic, even from the passenger seat of his wife's car, his body responds before his mind does. His hands go cold. His chest tightens. He has asked her to change routes without explaining why, and she has learned not to ask. At home, he is easily startled by unexpected sounds — a door closing too hard, a neighbour's raised voice — and his wife describes him as having become someone who is always braced for something. He knows she is right. He feels it constantly: a low, persistent readiness, as though the moment on that wall never fully ended.

Marcus carries a specific and corrosive shame about this. He is a middle-aged professional man in a stable life. He tells himself, repeatedly, that what happened was not the worst thing that happens to people. He knows this intellectually. But his body does not seem to know it. He has not filed any formal complaint because the thought of sitting across from anyone in authority — anyone with institutional power over him — produces a dread he cannot push through.

He came to therapy at his wife's urging, after she found him sitting in the kitchen at four in the morning, staring at the wall with the lights off. He sat across the desk in the first session with his hands folded tightly in his lap, and the first thing he said was that he wasn't sure he had the right to be there. That other people had it so much worse. He said it the way a man says something he has been arguing with himself about for a very long time.
